title: East and south
hook: parents and children, teachers and students: duties both ways
carry: respect flows up, care flows down

segments.voice: Yesterday: four false friends and four true ones. Your line: the friend in need. Today the Buddha turns Sigala back toward the sunrise.

Honor your father and mother. Respect your elders. Listen to your teacher. Rules like these point one way: from the young to the old. The Sigalovada does something worth noticing. Every time it tells the young man what he owes, it turns around and says what is owed to him. Five duties going one way, five coming back, for parents and for teachers alike. A bow in two directions.
screen: `FROM THE YOUNG TO THE OLD.` → `FIVE DUTIES EACH WAY.` → `A BOW IN TWO DIRECTIONS.`

segments.voice: East is the parents, the direction where the day begins. A child, the Buddha says, honors them in five ways, thinking: they supported me, so I'll support them. I'll do the work they need done. I'll keep up the family line. I'll be worthy of what they leave me. And when they've died, I'll make offerings in their memory. Parents, honored like this, show their love in five ways too. They keep their child from what's harmful, encourage what's good, have the child trained in a skill, help arrange a suitable marriage, and at the right time, hand over the inheritance. South is the teachers. A student honors a teacher by rising to greet them, by waiting on them, by being eager to learn, by small acts of service, and by taking the lesson seriously. The teacher in return trains the student well, makes sure they've really understood, teaches them the whole of the craft, speaks well of them to friends, and keeps them safe wherever they go. Notice the balance. The child's list ends with remembering parents after death; the parents' list ends with letting go of what they own at the right time. The student's list ends with attention; the teacher's with protection. Some details belong to ancient India, arranged marriages and inheritances. But the shape is plain. Respect flows up, care flows down, and when both flow, the direction is honored.
screen: `EAST: THEY SUPPORTED ME.` · `PARENTS: SKILL, MARRIAGE, INHERITANCE.` · `SOUTH: EAGER TO LEARN.` · `TEACHERS: THE WHOLE CRAFT, AND SAFETY.` · then, large: `EAST AND SOUTH.`

segments.voice: Turn, if you can, toward the east and bring to mind a parent, or whoever raised you, living or not, and quietly honor one thing they gave you. Then turn toward the south and bring to mind a teacher, a coach, a mentor, someone who showed you how, and let one lesson they gave you come up. If you have children or students yourself, notice the duties coming back the other way.
disa. In DN 31 the east is parents and the south is teachers, each with five duties owed and five returned. Today's word.
Your line: respect flows up, care flows down. Five duties each way, for parents and for teachers. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In some Buddhist countries children bow to their parents and students to their teachers at festivals such as Thailand's teacher-honoring ceremony, and families make offerings and merit in memory of parents who have died.

chat.says: Does that Buddhist advice to Sigala only list what kids owe their parents?
options: No; parents owe five things back, like training their child in a skill.
Yes; in that text duty only runs upward, from young to old.
No; it says parents and children owe each other nothing at all.
chat.meaning: In DN 31 duties run both ways: a child honors parents in five ways, and parents show their love in five ways; the same for teachers.
